title: Atorvastatin suppresses high-risk colorectal adenomas via reprogramming of lipid metabolism and Inhibition of stemness

sections.abstract:
As critical precursors to colorectal cancer (CRC), high-risk colorectal adenomas (HR-CRAs) lack effective chemopreventive strategies beyond endoscopic resection. We previously established a standardized protocol for culturing patient-derived HR-CRA organoids (HR-CRA-PDOs), creating a robust platform for targeted drug discovery in colorectal premalignancy. Bioinformatics investigation was conducted to unveil the significant dysregulation of lipid metabolism in HR-CRAs. HR-CRA-PDOs were primarily cultured and exposed to gradient concentrations of atorvastatin, with drug responses evaluated with high-throughput and high-content imaging and ATP-based viability assays. Parallel in vivo validation utilized AOM/DSS-induced mouse model under either normal or high-fat diets. Histological and molecular analyses were conducted to evaluate adenoma dynamics, apoptosis, and lipid metabolism-related gene and protein expressions. Bioinformatics analysis of GEO database ( GSE100179 and GSE161277 ) revealed that HR-CRAs are characterized by dysregulated lipid metabolism, particularly through the upregulation of fatty acid metabolism pathways. In vitro, atorvastatin significantly inhibited HR-CRA-PDO growth in a dose-dependent manner via apoptosis induction and proliferation arrest. Mechanistically, atorvastatin treatment led to significant alterations of gene expression in lipid metabolism pathways including ACOX1 , ACOX2 , FABP2 , NRG1 , PPAR-α and SREBF1 , concomitant with stemness marker suppression in HR-CRA-PDOs. In vivo, atorvastatin markedly reduced CRA burden in AOM-DSS-induced mouse model, particularly demonstrating enhanced efficacy in high-fat diet contexts. This translational study establishes atorvastatin’s dual mechanism in metabolic reprogramming and stemness inhibition, suggesting its potential as a therapeutic strategy for CRA prevention and treatment.

The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1038/s41598-025-32406-y.

Keywords: Colorectal adenomas, Atorvastatin, Lipid metabolism, Patient-derived organoids, Cancer prevention

Subject terms: Cancer, Cell biology, Diseases, Gastroenterology
sections.introduction:
Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the third most common cancer worldwide and the second leading cause of cancer-related deaths 1 . It is estimated that around 85–90% of sporadic colorectal cancers develop from premalignant colorectal adenomas (CRA) 2 .The adenoma-to-carcinoma sequence involves abnormal proliferation of colon epithelial cells, with adenomas progressing based on the size and type of dysplasia 3 . Notably, those adenomas not less than 10 mm, or with villous or serrated morphology are commonly regarded as high-risk colorectal adenoma (HR-CRA), with a carcinogenesis rate of approximately 25% 4 . So far, the only clinical modality for CRA treatment is endoscopic polypectomy 5 . Nevertheless, despite its efficacy and widespread use, several factors impede the patient compliance with colonoscopy. These include the colonoscopy’s invasive and uncomfortable nature, as well as it high cost, which is particularly burdensome for individuals with recurrent or multiple CRAs 6 . Several drugs are currently being tested in clinical trials for CRA treatment, including the COX-2 selective inhibitor celecoxib 7 , nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs such as aspirin 8 and ibuprofen 9 , as well as berberine 10 . However, with unneglectable potential adverse effects such as cardiovascular toxicity and gastrointestinal ulceration and bleeding. Consequently, it is imperative to develop the efficacious pharmacological intervention strategies for CRAs that possess safety profiles more amenable to patient tolerance, which is also pivotal for the secondary prevention of CRC.

Unhealthy lifestyle-induced metabolic disorders, particularly fat accumulation, can significantly increase the incidence of CRC, partially through increased reactive oxygen species (ROS) production and activation of MAPK signaling pathways 11 , 12 . Meanwhile, previous studies have comprehensively delved into the significant impact of dysregulated lipid metabolism on the development of CRAs. Elevated triglycerides 13 , 14 , total cholesterol 15 , and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol 16 , as well as reduced high-density lipoprotein cholesterol 13 , are markedly associated with an increased risk of CRAs. Furthermore, obesity and metabolic abnormalities are shown to be linked to a higher risk of CRA recurrence 17 . However, whether targeting dysregulated lipid metabolism pathways can intervene the occurrence and progression of CRA remains uncertain.

Statins, including atorvastatin, lovastatin, simvastatin, and rosuvastatin, are inhibitors of 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl coenzyme A (HMG-CoA) reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme in the mevalonate pathway 18 . Widely used in clinical practice, these drugs are prescribed for the management of hyperlipidemia and cardiovascular risk, demonstrating both high efficacy and excellent safety profiles 19 . Over the past decades, studies have revealed that statins possess pleiotropic effects including inhibiting tumor growth inhibition and cancer cell apoptosis, which collectively suggest their broader therapeutic potential 20 – 23 . Evidence further suggests that statin use reduces cancer-related mortality by approximately 15%, with no apparent dose-response relationship 24 . Additionally, multiple meta-analyses have confirmed that statin therapy significantly decreases both all-cause and cancer-specific mortality in CRC patients 25 . These findings underscore the critical role of statins in cancer prevention and treatment, thereby prompting further investigation into their therapeutic efficacy in the management of CRAs.

Our prior study has developed a crucial methodology for culturing the patient-derived HR-CRA organoids (HR-CRA-PDOs), which serves as a reliable in vitro model for drug testing of CRAs and perfect for the current study 26 . Here, we further investigated the alterations in lipid metabolism pathways within CRAs, confirmed the efficacy of statins with both in vitro and in vivo models, and revealed the potential underlying mechanisms.
sections.methods:
Bulk transcriptomic data were downloaded from the GEO database ( GSE100179 , https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/ ) 27 . Following normalization, principal component analysis (PCA) was applied to distinguish global transcriptional differences between adenoma and normal tissues. Differentially expressed genes were identified using the limma package (v3.58.1), with inclusion criteria of average expression value > 1, fold change ≥ 1.5, and adjusted p-value < 0.05. Lipid metabolism–related genes were retrieved through literature mining, and volcano plots were generated to illustrate their expression patterns, resulting in the identification of 19 differentially expressed lipid metabolism genes. Heatmaps were used to visualize expression profiles across samples. Pathway enrichment analyses for Gene Ontology (GO) terms and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) 28 – 30 pathways were performed on the differentially expressed lipid metabolism–related genes using the clusterProfiler R package. The “enrichplot” and “ggplot2” packages were applied to visualize enrichment results. Additionally, protein–protein interaction (PPI) networks of the lipid metabolism–related genes were constructed to identify potential hub genes and regulatory interactions.

Single-cell transcriptomic data were obtained from the GEO database ( GSE161277 , https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/ ) 31 . The raw data were processed using the Seurat package (v5.2.1). Quality control was performed by retaining cells with nFeature_RNA > 300, nCount_RNA > 1000, and mitochondrial gene content < 20%. Doublets were removed using DoubletFinder (v2.0.6). Data normalization, dimensionality reduction, and clustering were conducted using default parameters, with the first 20 principal components (dims = 1:20) selected for downstream analyses. Cell type annotation was performed based on canonical marker genes. The clustering and cell-type annotation results were visualized by UMAP, while marker gene expression patterns were displayed using dot plots. Since our study primarily focused on epithelial cells in adenoma and normal intestinal tissues, epithelial subsets were extracted for further analysis. Differential gene expression between adenoma and normal epithelial cells was identified using the FindMarkers function in Seurat, with thresholds set at fold change ≥ 4 and adjusted p-value < 0.05. Functional enrichment analyses of differentially expressed genes were performed using the clusterProfiler package (v4.16.0), and pathways with p < 0.05 were considered significantly enriched.

Ten human adenoma biopsy samples were collected for research purposes, with approval from the Ethics Committee of Huashan Hospital, Fudan University (Approval No. 2013-005), and written informed consent was obtained from all patients, ensuring compliance with the Declaration of Helsinki guidelines. The CRA samples were cut into fragments of approximately 3 mm³ and washed three times with pre-cooled D-PBS buffer. The tissue fragments were digested in tumor digestion solution (bioGenous, K601010) at 37 °C for 30 min with vigorous shaking, after which three times of Advanced DMEM/F12 medium (vol/vol) was added to terminate the digestion. The mixture was centrifuged at 500×g for five minutes, and the supernatant was discarded. The isolated epithelial cells were mixed with Matrigel (Corning, 356231) and cultured as previously described 32 . The CRA culture medium consisted of a basal medium supplemented with growth factors and small molecules, including R-spondin1 (R&D, 4645-RS, 500 ng/mL), Noggin (PeproTech, 250 − 38, 100 ng/mL), EGF (R&D, 236-EG, 50 ng/mL), [Leu15]-gastrin I (Sigma-Aldrich, G9145, 10 nmol/L), SB202190 (Sigma-Aldrich, S7067, 10 µmol/L), and A-83-01 (Selleck, S7692, 500 nmol/L). The basal culture medium for CRA organoids was prepared using Advanced DMEM/F12 (Gibco, 12634010) supplemented with B27 (17504-044, 50×), N2 (17502-048, 100×), GlutaMAX-I (35050079, 100×) (Invitrogen), N-acetylcysteine (A9165, 1.25 mmol/L), Nicotinamide (N0636, 10 mmol/L) (Sigma-Aldrich), and 1% penicillin/streptomycin.

Culture medium was changed every other day. The organoids were passaged at a 1:3 ratio digested with TrypLE (Gibco, 12605028) solution when appropriate.

CRA organoids grown in 48-well plates were collected and resuspended in Matrigel. Then 2,000 organoid single cells were evenly seeded into 96-well plates (Corning, 3299) at 5 µL per well. Atorvastatin (TargetMol, T3116) was added to the culture medium at final concentrations of 1 µM, 3 µM, 10 µM, 30 µM, 100 µM, and 300 µM. Before drug treatment, the CRA organoids were cultured for 5 days. Following treatment with the specified concentrations of the compound for 3 days, organoids were stained with 5 µg/mL propidium iodide (PI) (YEASEN, 40711ES) and 10 µg/mL Hoechst 33,342 (YEASEN, 40731ES) to identify dead cells and nuclei, respectively. After 20 min of incubation, organoid images were captured using the Z-stack high-throughput imaging mode on the BZ-X800 microscope (Keyence, Japan). Additionally, CellTiter-Glo 3D cell viability assays were performed using the CellTiter-Glo 3D Cell Viability Assay Kit (Promega, G9682) to assess organoid viability according to the manufacturer’s instruction.

C57BL/6 mice were purchased from Yishang Biotechnology Co., Ltd. (Shanghai, China) and housed under specific pathogen-free (SPF) conditions. All animal experiments were conducted in accordance with relevant guidelines and were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) of Fudan University (2021JS-398). The procedures followed the Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals (8th Edition, 2011; https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK54050/ ) published by the National Institutes of Health.

AOM/DSS-induced colorectal adenoma mouse model was generated. Briefly, six-week-old male C57BL/6J mice were first injected with 10 mg/kg AOM intraperitoneally. One week later, mice were exposed to two cycles of DSS treatment (2% DSS in drinking water for 7 days followed by a 14-day recovery period). After the final round of DSS treatment, the mice were randomly divided into two groups and fed with either a normal diet or a high-fat diet (60% fat) for the duration of the study. After adenoma formation, each group of mice ( n = 9) was further randomized into two subgroups and treated for two weeks with either normal drinking water or atorvastatin (30 mg/kg/day) solution. The preparation of atorvastatin solution was as follows. Atorvastatin calcium was first dissolved in a minimal volume of 0.1 M NaOH, gently sonicated for 2–3 min until clear, and subsequently diluted with autoclaved drinking water to the desired final concentration (30 mg/kg/day equivalent). The pH of the resulting solution was carefully adjusted to 7.0–7.4.0.4, ensuring stability and compliance for long-term oral administration. At the end of the treatment, all the mice were euthanized overdose by intraperitoneal injection of sodium pentobarbital (Sigma-Aldrich, P3761) at a dose of 160 mg/kg, with colon tissues collected for the evaluation of the number, size, and pathological type of the colorectal tumors/adenomas.

Total RNA was extracted from CRA-PDOs using the RNA Extraction Kit (DP451, TIANGEN Biotech Co., Ltd., Beijing, China). First-strand cDNA was synthesized using the HiScript SuperMix (Vazyme) with 1 µg of purified RNA per reaction. Quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) was performed using SYBR Green (Vazyme) and primers listed in the supplementary table. Cq values were detected on a 7500 PCR system according to the manufacturer’s instructions for the qPCR kit, and fold changes were calculated using the 2 −ΔΔCt method with GAPDH as an internal control.

Mouse intestinal tissues were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA) for 12 h, embedded in paraffin, and sectioned into 7 μm slices. After antigen retrieval with citrate buffer solution (Vector Laboratories), the slides were blocked with 5% BSA and incubated overnight at 4 °C with primary antibodies. Corresponding secondary antibodies (Invitrogen) were diluted 1:400 in blocking buffer and incubated at room temperature for one hour.

The organoids were whole-mount immunostained as described 26 . Briefly, organoids were fixed in 4% PFA, permeabilized with 0.1% Triton X-100, and blocked with 5% BSA at room temperature. Primary antibodies were diluted in blocking buffer and incubated overnight at 4 °C. The primary antibodies and their respective dilutions are as follows: anti-c-caspase3 (CST, 1:200), anti-Ki67 (Abcam, 1:200), anti-PCNA (Abcam, 1:200), and anti-SREBP1 (SER, 1:500). The corresponding secondary antibodies (Invitrogen) were diluted 1:400 in blocking buffer and incubated at room temperature for 1 h. DAPI staining solution was used for nuclear counterstaining. The staining images were captured using a confocal microscope (OLYMPUS FV3000, Japan) and the fluorescence intensity was quantified by ImageJ software (NIH, USA) for the corresponding comparisons.

Mouse colon tissues were fixed in 4% PFA followed by routine dehydration, embedding and sectioning. Sections at 5 μm were subjected to routine deparaffinization and then immersed into hematoxylin at room temperature for five minutes and transferred into deionized water. The slides were then put under the running tap water for 10 min to allow the stain for development. The slides were then differentiated in 1% acidified ethanol for ten seconds, and afterwards rinsed in running tap water for ten minutes followed by rinsed in deionized water for another two min. Eosin was applied for 30 s. After staining, the sections were then step-wisely dehydrated, cleared and mounted for imaging.

To evaluate the effect of atorvastatin on organoid stemness and self-renewal capacity, the single-cell organoid formation (colonosphere) assay was performed using patient-derived high-risk colorectal adenoma (HR-CRA) organoids from five independent donors. Mature organoids were dissociated into single cells using TrypLE (Gibco, 12605028) for 5 minutes at 37 °C with gentle pipetting, followed by filtration through a 40 µm cell strainer to obtain a uniform single-cell suspension. Viable cells were counted using trypan blue exclusion, resuspended in Matrigel (Corning, 356231), and seeded at a density of 2,000 cells per well in 96-well plates (Corning, 3299). Cells were treated with 25 µM atorvastatin (TargetMol, T3116) or vehicle control starting from the day of plating (designated as day 0, D0). Organoids were cultured at 37 °C in a humidified incubator with 5% CO₂ for 6 days, and the medium was refreshed every two days. Bright-field images were acquired daily (D0–D6) using the Z-stack high-throughput imaging mode on a BZ-X800 microscope (Keyence, Japan). On day 6, organoid viability was assessed using the CellTiter-Glo 3D Cell Viability Assay Kit (Promega, G9682) according to the manufacturer’ s instructions. Luminescence intensity was measured to quantify cell viability, reflecting the metabolic activity of living organoids under each treatment condition.

To explore the relationship between lipid metabolism gene expression and atorvastatin sensitivity, ten patient-derived HR-CRA organoid lines (P1–P10) were analyzed. The qRT-PCR procedure was performed as described previously. Atorvastatin sensitivity was determined by determining IC50 values through a 7-point dose–response assay using the CellTiter-Glo 3D Cell Viability Assay (Promega, G9682). The correlation between gene expression and IC50 was evaluated using simple linear regression analysis in GraphPad Prism 10.0 (GraphPad Software, USA). The coefficient of determination (R²) and regression equations are shown in each plot. All assays were performed in biological triplicates.

Transient siRNA knockdown of ACOX1, FABP2, and SREBF1 was performed in patient-derived HR-CRA organoids to evaluate their functional contribution to the response to atorvastatin. Organoids were enzymatically dissociated using TrypLE (Gibco, 12605028) and resuspended in Opti-MEM medium (Gibco, 11058021) containing 50 nM siRNA (FUBIO, China) and Lipofectamine RNA iMAX (Invitrogen, 13778150). The transfection mixture was seeded into Matrigel domes (Corning, 356231) supplemented with 10 µM Y-27,632 (Selleck, S1049) and incubated for 72 h prior to drug treatment. Following transfection, organoids were treated with 25 µM atorvastatin or vehicle for 48 h. Knockdown efficiency was verified by quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) as described previously. Organoid viability after treatment was determined using the CellTiter-Glo 3D Cell Viability Assay (Promega, G9682) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Luminescence values were normalized to the control siRNA group to assess the effect of each gene on atorvastatin sensitivity.

All data are presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD). Statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism 9.3 software. For data that met the criteria of normal distribution and homogeneity of variance, comparisons between two groups were conducted using Student’s t -test, and two-way (ANOVA) was used for comparisons among multiple groups. (version 8; GraphPad Software, La Jolla, CA, USA). P -value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. *, P < 0.05; **, P < 0.01; ***, P < 0.001; ****, P < 0.0001.
sections.results:
Based on the data from GEO database ( GSE100179 ), the transcriptomic analysis identified a series of differentially expressed genes between colorectal adenoma ( n = 20) and normal mucosa ( n = 20), with a significant subset upregulated in adenoma tissues (Fig. 1 A). Principal component analysis (PCA) demonstrated clear separation between adenoma and normal samples, indicating distinct transcriptional profiles (Fig. 1 B). Heatmap analysis revealed consistent dysregulation of multiple lipid metabolism–related genes. Key genes such as SCD , ENPP2 , and PLAGL2 were markedly upregulated, while several others were downregulated (Fig. 1 C). These findings were further confirmed by the volcano plot analysis (Fig. 1 D). Venn diagram analysis identified an overlap of 19 genes between the differentially expressed genes (DEGs) and lipid metabolism–associated genes, suggesting lipid metabolic reprogramming as a prominent feature of adenoma (Fig. 1 E). Pathway enrichment analysis showed significant enrichment of these genes in fatty acid metabolism, PPAR signaling, glycolysis/gluconeogenesis, and cytochrome P450–mediated xenobiotic metabolism pathways (Fig. 1 F). Gene Ontology enrichment further indicated their involvement in fatty acid metabolic processes, lipid catabolic processes, lipoprotein particle organization, and oxidoreductase activity (Fig. 1 G). Finally, protein–protein interaction network analysis identified hub genes including ENPP2 , FABP2 , SCD , CPT1A and PLAGL2 , which formed a tightly interconnected network, suggesting their potential role as central regulators driving lipid metabolic reprogramming and promoting adenoma progression (Fig. 1 H).

Transcriptomic Alterations Reveal Lipid Metabolic Reprogramming in Colorectal Adenoma. The transcriptomic analysis was based on the GEO database ( GSE100179 ) including data generated from paired colorectal adenoma ( n = 20) and normal mucosa ( n = 20). (A) Distribution of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) between adenoma and normal mucosa. (B) Principal component analysis (PCA) showing clear separation of adenoma and normal samples. (C) Heatmap of representative lipid metabolism–related DEGs across datasets. (D) Volcano plot highlighting significantly upregulated and downregulated lipid metabolism genes. (E) Venn diagram showing 19 overlapping genes between DEGs and lipid metabolism–related genes. (F) KEGG pathway enrichment analysis indicating significant involvement of fatty acid metabolism, PPAR signaling, glycolysis/gluconeogenesis, and cytochrome P450 pathways 28 – 30 . (G) GO enrichment analysis revealing associations with fatty acid metabolic process, lipid catabolic process, lipoprotein particle organization, and oxidoreductase activity. (H) Protein–protein interaction (PPI) network of key lipid metabolism–related genes, with hub nodes ( ENPP2 , FABP2 , SCD , CPT1A , PLAGL2 ) highlighted.

To resolve cellular heterogeneity and pinpoint lipid metabolic dysregulation in colorectal adenoma, we obtained single-cell transcriptomic data from the GEO database ( GSE161277 ). Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) plots revealed distinct clustering of major epithelial and stromal cell types, including enterocytes, goblet cells, B cells, macrophages, fibroblasts, and malignant epithelial populations, which demonstrated compositional shifts in adenoma (Fig. 2 A). Expression distributions of canonical marker genes across cell subsets validated cluster identities and highlighted transcriptional diversity within the epithelial and immune compartments (Fig. 2 B). Functional enrichment analysis of DEGs implicated key lipid metabolism–related pathways including retinol metabolism, PPAR signaling, arachidonic acid metabolism, and glycerolipid metabolism, indicating broad remodeling of metabolic networks in adenoma cells (Fig. 2 C). Violin plot analyses further confirmed significant alterations in critical lipid metabolism–associated genes, including ACACB , DGAT1 , AGPAT1 , AGPAT3 , MLXIPL , ELOVL6 , LRP1 , LDLR , SCARB1 , GPAM , FASN , and FABP5 in adenomas versus normal tissues (Fig. 2 D). Collectively, these findings demonstrated that colorectal adenoma exhibits profound metabolic heterogeneity at single-cell resolution and robust activation of lipid metabolic pathways.

Single-cell transcriptomic profiling identifies lipid metabolism dysregulation in colorectal adenoma. The GEO database ( GSE161277 ) was utilized for analyses. (A) UMAP plots displaying distinct clustering of epithelial and stromal cell types in normal and adenoma tissues. (B) Dot plot showing marker gene distribution and expression across identified cell subsets. (C) KEGG pathway enrichment analysis of differentially expressed genes, highlighting significant enrichment in lipid metabolism–related pathways 28 – 30 . (D) Violin plots comparing expression levels of representative lipid metabolism–related genes ( ACACB , DGAT1 , AGPAT1 , AGPAT3 , MLXIPL , ELOVL6 , LRP1 , LDLR , SCARB1 , GPAM , FASN , FABP5 ) between normal and adenoma samples.

To evaluate the efficacy of atorvastatin on inhibition of HR-CRA, the patient-derived HR-CRA organoids (HR-CRA-PDOs) were constructed as published before by our research group as shown in Fig. 3 A 26 . These HR-CRA-PDOs exhibited stable growth in a 3D culture system, providing a reliable in vitro model for drug screening and mechanism investigation.

Atorvastatin significantly inhibits the growth of HR-CRA organoids in a concentration-dependent manner. Patient-derived HR-CRA organoids (HR-CRA-PDOs) were established for drug screening. (A) The schematic display of HR-CRA-PDO construction. Bright-field images showing 4-day culture of HR-CRA-PDO organoids. Scale bar, 500 μm. (B) Each well was initially seeded with 2,000 organoid single cells. Bright-field images, propidium iodide (PI)-Hoechst 33,342 staining of HR-CRA-PDOs after treatment with gradient concentrations of atorvastatin (0, 1, 3, 10, 30, 100, 300 µM) for three days. PI staining (red) indicates dead cells. Scale bar, 500 μm. (C) Each well was initially seeded with 2,000 organoid single cells. The combined dose-dependent response curves of atorvastatin treatment on HR-CRA-PDOs from ten patients (P1-P10), with an average IC50 of 25 µM. Data represent the mean ± SD.

With HR-CRA-PDOs, we explored the efficacy of atorvastatin to inhibit HR-CRA by conducting high-throughput and high-content drug testing. The HR-CRA-PDOs were first digested and seeded into 96-well plate, and allowed to grow for four days. After that, atorvastatin at the concentrations of 0, 1, 3, 10, 30, 100, 300 µM were applied to the HR-CRA-PDOs. Three days later, the bright-field images were captured and propidium iodide (PI) staining (red staining, which indicates dead cells) were performed. The results revealed a clear dose-dependent increase in the number of dead cells within the PDOs as atorvastatin concentration rose, suggesting the significant inhibition effect of atorvastatin on HR-CRA-PDOs (Fig. 3 B). To address the issue of heterogeneity, we assessed the efficacy of atorvastatin in HR-CRA-PDOs from ten patients (P1-P10) in total. Consequently, all the HR-CRA-PDOs demonstrated a potent dose-dependent response to atorvastatin, with the average IC50 of 25 µM (Fig. 3 C, Supplementary Fig. 1). These findings indicate that atorvastatin can effectively inhibit the growth of HR-CRA-PDOs and induce HR-CRA cell death in vitro.

To elucidate the specific growth-inhibitory effects of atorvastatin on HR-CRA-PDOs, we conducted comprehensive analyses focusing on the proliferation, stemness and apoptosis of HR-CRA-PDOs following atorvastatin treatment at 25 µM (Fig. 4 ). With PI and Hoechst 33,342 staining, the immunofluorescent staining results revealed that atorvastatin significantly increased cell death within HR-CRA-PDOs (Fig. 4 A). Consistently, the expression of cleaved-caspase-3 is markedly elevated in atorvastatin-treated HR-CRA-PDOs, suggesting the enhanced cell apoptosis (Figure. 4B). Simultaneously, EdU staining results showed that atorvastatin markedly suppressed cell proliferation in the PDOs (Fig. 4 C), which is aligned with the decreased Ki67 staining after atorvastatin treatment (Fig. 4 D). Statistical analysis of the immunofluorescence staining data further corroborated the aforementioned findings (Fig. 4 E). Moreover, as the cell proliferation of organoids is closely associated with the stemness, the RT-qPCR results demonstrated that atorvastatin notably downregulated the expression of stemness-associated genes including OLFM4 , SOX9 and LGR5 as compared to the control group (Fig. 4 F). To determine whether atorvastatin impairs stemness and self-renewal, single-cell organoid formation assays were performed using HR-CRA organoids from three donors (P1–P3). The results demonstrated that organoids treated with 25 µM atorvastatin exhibited markedly reduced sphere number and size compared with vehicle controls. Quantitative analysis of viability confirmed a significant decrease in organoid survival, indicating that atorvastatin directly suppresses stemness and regenerative capacity (Supplementary Fig. 2 A). Collectively, these findings indicate that atorvastatin exerts growth-inhibitory effects on HR-CRA-PDOs by inducing cell apoptosis and downregulating proliferation.

Atorvastatin hinders the growth of HR-CRA-PDOs by promoting apoptosis, and inhibiting proliferation and stemness. Each well was seeded with 2,000 organoid single cells. After five days, HR-CRA-PDOs were treated with 25 µM atorvastatin for three days. (A) Propidium iodide (PI) and Hoechst 33,342 staining. PI staining (red) indicates dead cells. Scale bar, 500 μm. (B) Immunofluorescence staining of cleaved-caspase-3. Scale bar, 100 μm. (C) EdU staining. Scale bar, 100 μm. (D) Ki67 immunostaining. Scale bar, 100 μm. (E) The percentage of immunofluorescent positive cells in B, C and D was analyzed for comparison. (F) RT-qPCR analysis of stemness-associated genes, including OLFM4 , SOX9 , and LGR5 . Data represent the mean ± SD and subjected to Student’s t -test. **, P < 0.01; ***, P < 0.001; ****, P < 0.0001.

As shown in Fig. 1 , abnormal lipid metabolism could be a critical driver in the initiation and progression of CRAs. Given this context, we explored the mechanisms underlying atorvastatin’s effects in HR-CRA-PDOs by examining changes in the expression of lipid metabolism-related genes. The results displayed that, compared to the control group, several key genes involved in lipid metabolism were significantly downregulated in the atorvastatin-treated group, including ACOX1 , ACOX2 , FABP2 , and NRG1 (Fig. 5 A). These genes are implicated in fatty acid synthesis, oxidation, transport, and nuclear receptor regulation, suggesting that atorvastatin may reduce adenoma formation risk by suppressing its lipid metabolism activity. Additionally, the expression of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha ( PPARα ) was found to be markedly upregulated in the atorvastatin-treated group. This finding indicated that atorvastatin may maintain lipid metabolic balance by modulating fatty acid oxidation and energy production, thereby inhibiting adenoma growth (Fig. 5 B). Notably, SREBF1 is a key transcription factor that maintains lipid homeostasis, which is responsible for activating genes associated with triglyceride, fatty acid and cholesterol synthesis. RT-qPCR and immunofluorescence analysis revealed that atorvastatin significantly suppressed the mRNA and protein expression of SREBF1 in HR-CRA PDOs (Fig. 5 C and D), further supporting its role in regulating lipid metabolism. To confirm the involvement of lipid-metabolic pathways in atorvastatin response, we performed siRNA-mediated knockdown of SREBF1 , FABP2 , and ACOX1 in HR-CRA organoids (Supplementary Fig. 3 A). qRT-PCR confirmed efficient gene silencing (Supplementary Fig. 3B). Functional assays revealed that knockdown of each gene partially rescued organoid growth during atorvastatin exposure, with SREBF1 silencing showing the most pronounced reduction in atorvastatin sensitivity, followed by FABP2 and ACOX1 , suggesting their cooperative role in mediating the growth-inhibitory effects of atorvastatin (Supplementary Fig. 3 C). Moreover, we explored the molecular basis of inter-patient variability in atorvastatin response, we quantified the expression of lipid metabolism–related genes including ACOX1 , FABP2 and SREBF1 across ten patient-derived HR-CRA organoids. qRT-PCR revealed heterogeneous expression levels among organoid lines. Linear regression analysis demonstrated positive correlations between the expression of all three genes and the corresponding IC50 values, suggesting that higher baseline lipid metabolic activity is associated with reduced atorvastatin sensitivity (Supplementary Fig. 4).

Atorvastatin modulates lipid metabolism-related gene expression in HR-CRA-PDOs. HR-CRA-PDOs were treated with 25 µM atorvastatin for three days. (A) RT-qPCR analysis of key lipid metabolism-related genes including ACOX1 , ACOX2 , and NRG1. (B) RT-qPCR analysis of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha ( PPARα ). (C) RT-qPCR analysis of SREBF1 . (D) The intensity of immunofluorescence staining of SREBF1 was analyzed for comparison. Scale bar, 100 μm. Data represent the mean ± SD and subjected to Student’s t -test. *, P < 0.05; **, P < 0.01; ***, P < 0.001; ****, P < 0.0001.

To investigate whether the inhibitory effects of atorvastatin on adenoma growth are also evident in vivo, we established an AOM/DSS-induced mouse model to resemble the occurrence of colonic adenomas with six-week-old male C57BL/6J mice 33 . Meanwhile, given that lipid dysregulation plays a crucial role in the progression of HR-CRA, we simultaneously administered a high-fat diet (HFD) to partial mice to evaluate the efficacy of atorvastatin. Following 10 mg/kg AOM injection and two rounds of 2% DSS with or without HFD feeding, the mice were divided into four groups to observe the therapeutic potential of atorvastatin on colonic adenoma formation and development (Supplementary Fig. 5 A). During treatment, the mouse body weight was recorded. While high-fat diet challenge resulted in increased body weight as compared to the normal chow groups, atorvastatin treatment led to no significant alterations of body weight in neither group (Supplementary Fig. 5B). Colon length measurements revealed that HFD groups had a significantly shorter colon compared to the normal chow groups, with atorvastatin treatment demonstrated a slightly increasing trend in both groups (Fig. 6 A and B). In both normal chow and HFD groups, atorvastatin significantly reduced the incidence of adenomas (Fig. 6 C), particularly for the high-grade adenomas that are larger than 2 mm in size (Fig. 6 D and E). Notably, HFD treatment promoted the formation of adenoma and reduced the efficacy of atorvastatin. The results were further confirmed by the histological examination. H&E staining results confirmed the tissue-protective effects of atorvastatin, with treated mice exhibiting significantly reduced lesion severity and more regular glandular structures compared to control group with the same chow (Fig. 6 F, upper and middle panel). Immunofluorescence analysis further demonstrated a notable reduction in the expression of the proliferation marker PCNA in the atorvastatin-treated group (Fig. 6 F, lower panel; Fig. 6 G), indicating that atorvastatin exerts its anti-adenoma effects by inhibiting cell proliferation. In summary, these results suggest that atorvastatin can effectively inhibit adenoma growth in vivo.

sections.discussion:
In this study, we uncovered that the lipid metabolism pathway is significantly upregulated in CRAs as compared to normal mucosa tissues (Fig. 1 ), which inspired us to propose statins as potential therapeutic candidates for CRA intervention. With HR-CRA-PDOs and AOM/DSS-induced mouse CRA model, we proved the efficacy of atorvastatin in CRA inhibition both in vitro and in vivo, highlighting the potential of targeting lipid metabolism as a therapeutic strategy for CRA prevention and treatment.

Emerging evidence positions dysregulated lipid metabolism as a pivotal driver in CRA pathogenesis through multiple pathways 4 . Beyond its established role in adenoma initiation, abnormal lipid homeostasis promotes carcinogenic processes via sustained oxidative stress and chronic inflammation, which collectively induce genetic mutations and genomic instability 34 . Notably, the overexpression of key lipid metabolic enzymes, including fatty acid synthase (FASN) and 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl coenzyme A reductase (HMGCR), correlates with advanced tumor progression and unfavorable prognosis in CRC patients 35 . These mechanistic insights reveal promising therapeutic targets for secondary CRC prevention, particularly through strategic modulation of lipid biosynthesis pathways and precise regulation of fatty acid oxidation processes.

Organoids, three-dimensional (3D) miniature organs cultured in vitro, are increasingly utilized in biomedical research to model disease mechanisms and evaluate drug efficacy 36 . In colorectal adenoma research, organoids have emerged as an innovative in vitro model that overcomes many limitations of traditional approaches 26 . With just a small amount of adenoma tissue, epithelial cells can be isolated and expanded to form 3D structures resembling the original tissue 32 . These organoids not only preserve the gene expression profiles of the primary tumor over extended periods, but also maintain intratumoral cellular heterogeneity, accurately representing the responses of tumor epithelial cells to drugs 37 . Furthermore, organoids exhibit robust expansion capabilities and shorter experimental timelines, making them highly suitable for large-scale, high-throughput drug screening, thereby offering a reliable tool for drug development 38 . Patient-derived organoids, in particular, has been leveraged as a clinically predictive in vitro model that bridges interpatient heterogeneity and therapeutic responsiveness 39 . Despite inherent variations in drug responses across individual HR-CRA-PDOs derived from 10 patients, atorvastatin demonstrated consistent growth-inhibitory effects in all HR-CRA-PDOs (Fig. 2 ). As our previous study shown, the abnormally elevated stemness is the key genomic feature of HR-CRA-PDOs 26 , atorvastatin treatment significantly suppressed both stemness markers and proliferative capacity (Fig. 3 ). Meanwhile, atorvastatin can markedly regulate lipid metabolism reflected by the altered key genes including ACOX1 , ACOX2 , FABP2 , NRG1 , SREBF1 and PPARα (Fig. 4 ). These mechanistic insights position atorvastatin as a promising candidate for CRC secondary prevention by simultaneously eradicating precancerous stem-like cell population and addressing metabolic dysregulation in CRA.

To refine inter-patient variability, we quantified atorvastatin IC50 across an expanded set of HR-CRA-PDOs and found consistent growth inhibition, while the correlation analyses revealed that the baseline expression of lipid-metabolism genes including ACOX1 , FABP2 and SREBF1 was positively associated with IC50, indicating that lipid-metabolic heterogeneity modulates pharmacologic response 40 . To further substantiate stemness as a key target of atorvastatin, we performed single-cell–derived organoid formation assays in five HR-CRA-PDO lines; atorvastatin (25 µM) significantly reduced spheroid-formation efficiency over six days, indicating impaired self-renewal and clonogenic capacity 41 . This functional phenotype is concordant with the reduction of stemness markers including OLFM4 , LGR5 and SOX9 .

Atorvastatin is lipophilic with high plasma-protein binding capacity and extensive first-pass hepatic extraction, leading to hepatic enrichment and extrahepatic exposure via systemic circulation and biliary excretion, which provides a plausible route for colonic epithelial exposure through enterohepatic recycling 42 . For the in vitro studies, the dose-response curve in Fig. 3 C demonstrated the average IC50 of Atorvastatin is 25 µM, a concentration within the commonly applied range for in vitro models investigating mevalonate-pathway dependence 43 , 44 . Meanwhile, the observed, dose-related growth inhibition with down-regulation of ACOX1 , FABP2 , and SREBF1 supports the on-target engagement rather than nonspecific toxicity 40 . In vivo, 30 mg/kg falls within the commonly used range in murine chemoprevention, which approximates a human-equivalent dose of about 2.4 mg/kg after body-surface-area correction (about 145 mg/day for a 60 kg adult), which exceeds the standard clinical doses of atorvastatin (10–20 mg/day, with 80 mg/day as the approved maximum) but should be appropriate for proof-of-mechanism studies 45 . It should be noted that rodent-human dose conversion does not account for major species differences in oral bioavailability, hepatic extraction, intestinal distribution, and OATP-mediated transport, all of which can lead to substantially lower effective exposure in mice relative to humans. Importantly, this dosage yielded coherent pharmacodynamic signatures including reduced adenoma burden and decreased PCNA without observable side effects. Future studies will incorporate lower oral doses, pharmacokinetic profiling and luminal exposure measurements to determine the minimal effective dose and better align the preclinical dosing with clinically achievable statin concentrations.

Statins are widely recognized for their cholesterol-lowering properties and are commonly used as preventive and therapeutic agents for cardiovascular diseases, offering remarkable efficacy with minimal adverse effects 46 . Increasing evidence suggests that the benefits of statins extend beyond their cardiovascular applications 47 . Cholesterol-derived metabolites play crucial roles in cellular proliferation by supporting essential functions such as membrane stability, signal transduction, protein synthesis, and cell cycle regulation 48 . Dysregulation of these processes in malignant cells disrupts tumor growth and metastasis 49 . Notably, the mevalonate pathway, a key cholesterol biosynthesis pathway, is frequently upregulated in cancers with mutated tumor suppressor protein p53 50 , which can be reversed by statins 50 . Moreover, studies have linked statin use to reduced mortality in cancers such as breast 51 , prostate 52 , colorectal 53 , and renal cell carcinoma 54 . The protective mechanisms of statins may involve the inhibition of oncogenic pathways, including MYC, AKT, and NF-κB, resulting in enhanced cytokine production, such as interleukin-6 (IL-6), tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), and transforming growth factor-β1 (TGF-β1) 55 . Additionally, it was reported that CRC-PDOs with high YAP expression exhibit greater sensitivity to atorvastatin, suggesting its therapeutic potential in YAP-overexpressing tumors 56 . In elderly patients diagnosed with rectal cancer, statin use has been associated with significant reductions in all-cause and cancer-specific mortality 57 . Since HR-CRA represents a precursor lesion to CRC, the intervention of HR-CRA through atorvastatin therapy is clinically rational and practicable.

From a translational perspective, patients with high metabolic burden especially those with obesity, metabolic syndrome, or habitual high-fat and red/processed-meat intake may derive greater chemopreventive benefit from atorvastatin due to heightened lipid-metabolic flux and pro-inflammatory signaling in the colorectal epithelium 58 , 59 . Perturbations in cholesterol homeostasis and mevalonate-dependent signaling in APC/KRAS-altered contexts, including PCSK9-linked pathways, further suggest that metabolically stressed adenomas could be particularly statin-responsive 60 . To optimize dosage decisions, a step-wise and safety-focused approach is advisable which initiate with moderate-intensity atorvastatin (10–20 mg daily) with the option to titrate to 40 mg in high-risk metabolic profiles if tolerated, accompanied by regular monitoring of liver enzymes ALT/AST and creatine kinase 43 . Integrating dietary modification (e.g., limiting processed/red meats and increasing fiber) with metabolic risk management may further activate epithelial pathways and improve long-term safety 59 .

Nevertheless, the long-term use of statins in HR-CRA populations warrants caution due to several known adverse effects. The most commonly reported complication is statin-associated muscle symptoms (SAMS) including myalgia 61 – 64 . Mild elevations of liver transaminases are also observed in a small subset of patients, though clinically significant liver injury remains rare 65 . Drug–drug interactions (e.g., with gemfibrozil) and pharmacogenomic variability (e.g., SLCO1B1 polymorphisms) can further influence statin tolerability and efficacy 63 . These side effects highlight the need for careful patient stratification, dose optimization and long-term safety monitoring in future clinical applications of statins in HR-CRA prevention. Pharmacologically, the lipophilicity of statins may endow them with distinct tissue penetration capabilities, which in turn significantly influence their drug efficacy. This characteristic provides valuable insights for the selection of the optimal statin drug. Moreover, nanoparticle-encapsulated statin formulations have the potential to enhance localized drug delivery while minimizing systemic side effects, representing a promising strategy to hinder colitis-associated carcinogenesis.

Collectively, these findings demonstrate that atorvastatin exerts multi-level chemopreventive effects against colorectal adenomas by suppressing lipid metabolic reprogramming, stemness and proliferative signaling. Clinical implementation should therefore incorporate metabolic risk stratification, pharmacogenomic profiling, and lifestyle-dietary synergy to maximize preventive efficacy.
sections.conclusion: To summarize, we demonstrated that atorvastatin inhibits the growth of HR-CRAs both in vitro and in vivo. Mechanistically, atorvastatin treatment significantly reduced organoid proliferation and stemness while promoting cell apoptosis, as well as regulating lipid metabolism pathways. These findings collectively suggest that statins hold significant potential as a preventive and therapeutic strategy for colorectal adenomas.
